title: Exploring students’ AI literacy and its effects on their AI output quality, self-efficacy, and academic performance
extended_summary:
This paper investigates how different dimensions of AI literacy relate to students’ AI self-efficacy, perceived AI output quality, and academic performance. The authors focus on three main components of AI literacy—technical understanding, practical application, and critical appraisal—and test whether these predict self-efficacy, output quality, and academic performance. The study is motivated by conflicting claims in the literature about whether AI tools help or harm student learning.

The study does not evaluate a ChatGPT writing intervention, randomized trial, or treatment-control experiment. Instead, it uses a quantitative online survey and structural equation modeling to examine associations among self-reported constructs. The measures assess students’ beliefs and experiences with AI generally, not a specific classroom writing-feedback program. Outcomes include self-reported academic performance, AI self-efficacy, and perceived AI output quality rather than experimentally observed changes in motivation or writing achievement.

Participants were 286 university students in Austria drawn by convenience sampling from five higher education institutions across three federal states. The sample included students in teacher education, elementary pedagogy, secondary teacher education, economics, digital education, and other pedagogical fields, spanning typical university-age students and older adult learners. The setting was an online survey context rather than a classroom intervention.

The main findings are that AI technical understanding and practical application positively predict AI self-efficacy, practical application positively predicts perceived AI output quality, and critical appraisal negatively predicts both self-efficacy and output quality. None of the AI literacy dimensions, self-efficacy, or output quality significantly predicted academic performance. For the user’s verification task: this paper is not the alleged 2026 high-school ChatGPT writing randomized controlled trial with 25+25 students over 12 weeks, reports no motivation outcome, no writing pre/post experiment, no random assignment, and no effect size near d = 19. It should not be treated as the target study for quantitative synthesis of ChatGPT-based writing feedback in high school and is not eligible for such a synthesis.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed correlational survey study using SEM with n=286 university students, not a randomized or quasi-experimental evaluation. It provides useful associations but does not meet causal evidence standards for intervention effectiveness.
impact_tier_rationale: For academic performance, the study reports essentially no impact of AI-related factors, and it does not evaluate a concrete ChatGPT writing-feedback intervention. Therefore it offers no credible positive impact estimate for quantitative synthesis.

interventions.use_case: Cross-sectional survey of university students’ general AI literacy, practical use of AI tools (including mentions of ChatGPT and AI for writing/feedback), and associations with AI self-efficacy, perceived AI output quality, and self-reported academic performance. This is not an intervention trial and does not test a specific writing-feedback program.

finding.finding_summary: Among Austrian university students (n=286), AI technical understanding positively predicted AI self-efficacy (β=0.441, p<0.001) and AI practical application also positively predicted AI self-efficacy (β=0.705, p<0.001), while AI critical appraisal negatively predicted AI self-efficacy (β=-0.348, p=0.016). The paper is correlational/SEM-based, not experimental, and reports no standardized between-group treatment effect sizes or confidence intervals for an intervention.
finding.measure: AI self-efficacy survey scale analyzed via structural equation modeling

finding.finding_summary: Perceived AI output quality was positively associated with AI practical application (β=0.599, p=0.005) and AI self-efficacy (β=0.229, p=0.029), but negatively associated with AI critical appraisal (β=-0.571, p=0.002); AI technical understanding had no significant effect (β=0.052, p=0.572). This reflects perceived quality/effectiveness/productivity of AI-supported work rather than measured performance gains from a writing-feedback intervention.
finding.measure: Perceived AI output quality scale analyzed via SEM

finding.finding_summary: The study found no significant effects of AI technical understanding (β=-0.158, p=0.096), AI critical appraisal (β=0.343, p=0.081), AI practical application (β=0.035, p=0.874), AI self-efficacy (β=0.116, p=0.271), or AI output quality (β=0.004, p=0.955) on students’ academic performance. Academic performance was self-reported and the paper provides no intervention-comparison statistics, no pre/post design, and no effect sizes suitable for synthesis of ChatGPT writing-feedback impacts.
finding.measure: Self-reported academic performance scale analyzed via SEM

finding.finding_summary: AI critical appraisal was modeled as an important construct and showed negative associations with AI self-efficacy (β=-0.348, p=0.016) and AI output quality (β=-0.571, p=0.002), but it had no significant relationship with academic performance (β=0.343, p=0.081). This captures students’ evaluative stance toward AI rather than a direct intervention effect on critical thinking skills.
finding.measure: AI critical appraisal survey construct within SEM
